0: Everything you need to understand why your GPU sits idle under load and which batching strategy fixes it. Three strategies from first principles, the flaw each one leaves behind, chunked prefill, and how to choose for your workload.
1: A modern GPU can run trillions of floating-point operations every second. Serving an LLM on one, you will often watch it sit at a small fraction of that.
2: The reason is that generating a single token means reading every weight in the model out of memory. That read dominates the time, and the compute units spend most of it waiting.
3: Batching closes the gap. Load the weights once, push many sequences through the same pass, and the memory cost gets spread across all of them.
4: Every serving engine does this. What separates them is when the batch gets decided.
5: Static decides once, before the batch starts
7: Continuous decides again at every forward pass
8: That last one is where nearly all the throughput in modern serving comes from. The other two are worth understanding first, since each fails in a way the next is built to fix.
9: And today we are going to break down and understand each of them one by one.
12: An A100 does roughly 312 teraFLOPs of BF16 math per second and moves about 2 terabytes per second out of memory. Decoding leans entirely on the second number.
13: Reading the weights is the whole cost, and the compute sits idle waiting. That idle compute is free capacity, so a batch of sixty rides the same weight read as the batch of one did, and throughput climbs while the memory read time stays the same.
14: Note that, throughput climbs steeply with batch size, then flattens.
15: Below the bend you are memory bound, and batching is close to free
16: Above it you are compute bound, and each added sequence costs time
17: The bend moves with the model, the GPU, and the sequence length, so measure it on your own hardware.
18: Now, you might be thinking: if batching is this effective, why not batch as much as possible?
19: Well, with LLMs, that is harder than it sounds. Let’s understand why.
21: Batching is older than LLMs. For a classifier or an embedding model, it is a packing problem.
22: Pad the inputs to a common length, stack them into one tensor, run one pass.
23: That works because three things hold. One pass produces the whole answer, no row depends on another, and every row's cost is known before it starts.
24: This doesn't work for autoregressive LLMs.
26: One pass produces one token, not the answer. A 400-token reply needs 400 forward passes.
27: Rows depend on their own history. Each pass writes into that request's KV cache, which the next pass reads back.
28: Cost is unknown until it is over. The model decides by emitting a stop token, which can after 12 tokens or after 4,000.
29: Padding does not rescue this. It equalizes input width, not how long a request holds the GPU.
